How to use the R package arulesViz from Python using arulespy¶

This document also runs directly in Google Colab.

Installation¶

This notebook needs arulespy installed and R set up (see Installation section on arulespy GitHub page). On Google Colab, only arulespy needs to be installed by uncomment the installation instruction in following code block:

In [14]:
# %pip install arulespy

Import Data and Mine Rules¶

Import the arules module from package arulespy.

In [15]:
from arulespy.arules import Transactions, apriori, parameters
from arulespy.arulesViz import inspect_dt, plot

We read Zoo.cvs which contains the description of 101 animals containing nominal variables and one quantitative variable as a pandas dataframe.

In [16]:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('Zoo.csv')

Convert the pandas dataframe into a sparse transactions object.

In [17]:
trans = Transactions.from_df(df)

trans.as_df()

In [18]:
rules = apriori(trans,
                    parameter = parameters({"supp": 0.1, "conf": 0.8}), 
                    control = parameters({"verbose": False}))  

rules.as_df().round(2)

arulesViz with ggplot¶

arulesViz provides ggplot as an drawing engine. arulesViz.plot() returns the ggplot object which can be included in the notebook using image_png().

In [19]:
import rpy2.robjects.lib.ggplot2 as gp
from rpy2.ipython.ggplot import image_png
In [20]:
gg = plot(rules, method="scatter")
image_png(gg)

R callback write-console: To reduce overplotting, jitter is added! Use jitter = 0 to prevent jitter.
  
R callback write-console: In addition:   
R callback write-console: Warning message:
  
R callback write-console: Column(s) 13, 17 not logical or factor. Applying default discretization (see '? discretizeDF').
Out[20]:
In [21]:
gg = plot(rules, method="grouped")
image_png(gg)
Out[21]:
In [22]:
rules_20 = rules.sort(by = 'confidence')[0:100]
gg = plot(rules_20, method="graph")
image_png(gg)
Out[22]:

Interactive Rules Table with HTML Widget¶

arulesViz can create interactive HTML widgets that can be integrated into a Python notebook by saving the widget as a self-contained HTML file and embedding its contents in an iframe. The html_widget helper makes this easy.

In [23]:
from arulespy.arulesViz import html_widget
In [24]:
m = inspect_dt(rules)
html_widget(m, "datatable.html", height=600)
Out[24]:

arulesViz with HTML Widgets¶

In [25]:
m = plot(rules_20, method="graph", engine="htmlwidget")
html_widget(m, "graph.html", height=800)
Out[25]:

Interactive RuleExplorer¶

Rule Explorer only has experimental support at this point. The rule_explorer() function opens a Shiny app in the web browser. Shutting down the Shiny app from within a Python notebook seems to be difficult. Uncomment the following line to explore the rules.

In [26]:
from arulespy.arulesViz import rule_explorer

# rule_explorer(rules)

An example of a running Rule Explorer can be found here.
